notes.meaning: Zechariah looks up and sees a man holding a measuring line. This builder is preparing to mark out Jerusalem's dimensions for restoration and growth. Many commentators understand this man to be the Angel of the Lord or the Messiah himself, who oversees the building of his people.

The prophet asks the man where he is going, and the man answers that he is measuring Jerusalem's width and length. This measurement shows that God has an exact plan to rebuild the city and make room for its people. It brought great comfort to the returned exiles, proving that their ruined city had a bright future.

The angel who has been talking with Zechariah steps forward, and another angel comes out to meet him. This second messenger brings fresh instructions from God about Jerusalem. The angels move with speed and eagerness to carry out the Lord's will.

The angel tells the messenger to run and give Zechariah an encouraging message. Jerusalem will grow so full of people and livestock that stone walls will not be able to hold them all. The city will spread out freely into the countryside like unwalled villages because of God's blessing.

differ.view: John Gill taught that this promise does not describe the literal city of Jerusalem, but refers spiritually to the worldwide spread of the church under the gospel.
Some evangelicals see this prophecy being fulfilled today in the modern physical expansion of Jerusalem far beyond its ancient walls.

notes.meaning: Jerusalem will not need stone walls for defense because the Lord promises to be an unapproachable wall of fire all around it. He will also live inside the city, filling it with his own divine honor and presence. Just as God guided Israel with fire in the desert, he will keep his people completely safe.

God calls out loudly for his people to escape from Babylon in the north and return home. Although the Lord had scattered them to every corner of the earth in his anger, he is now ready to gather them back. The exiles who had settled into comfortable lives are warned to leave before judgment falls on their captors.

The Lord urges his people, whom he calls Zion, to flee quickly from Babylon. God's holy people do not belong in a pagan land that is marked for destruction. Believers are summoned to leave behind worldly captivity and embrace the spiritual freedom God provides.

The Lord of hosts sends his divine messenger to judge the nations that plundered his people. Harming God's chosen people is like poking the pupil of his own eye, which is the most sensitive and fiercely guarded part of the body. This vivid picture shows how dearly God loves his children and how swiftly he will defend them.

differ.view: John Calvin taught that the apple of God's eye refers to the church as Christ's spiritual body, rather than only to the physical nation.
Some evangelicals believe the apple of God's eye refers directly to the Jewish people and the modern nation of Israel today.

notes.meaning: God will simply wave his hand, and the powerful enemy nations will collapse without a struggle. The oppressors will end up being plundered by the very people they once held as slaves. When this dramatic rescue happens, everyone will recognize that the Lord of hosts truly sent his messenger.

God commands his people to sing and celebrate with great joy because he is coming to live right among them. This promise was fulfilled when God's presence returned to the temple, and it reached a higher fulfillment when Jesus took on human flesh. God's dwelling with his people brings deep peace and reason to rejoice.

Many foreign nations will turn to the Lord and become his people alongside Israel. God's dwelling among this enlarged family will prove that the Lord of hosts has sent his divine messenger. Through this gathering, God's kingdom expands far beyond one nation to include all who trust him.

differ.view: Adam Clarke taught that this verse is fulfilled in the Christian church as whole Gentile nations embrace the gospel of Christ.
Some evangelicals hold that this refers to the future earthly reign of Christ in Jerusalem during the millennium.

notes.meaning: The Lord promises to claim Judah as his special inheritance and to choose Jerusalem once again. Even though his people had suffered exile and loss, God never cancelled his covenant love for them. Calling Canaan the Holy Land reminds the people that any place where God chooses to dwell is sacred.

Every person on earth is summoned to stand in silent reverence before the Lord. God is pictured as waking up and stepping out of his heavenly dwelling to take action and defend his people. His followers should quietly trust him, while his enemies must stop their proud speech.
